turns.text: The memory that still weighs on me is the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I had not been present the night before, when my name was shouted in front of the university for “persecuting” Mao Zedong’s daughter. I had only argued with her—never insulted her or treated her unfairly—but those differences in thought became ammunition. When I came back, students dragged me onto a stage, shouting, hitting, forcing me to bow. I remember the spit on my face, the fists in my back, the way my words—words I had always trusted—meant nothing. I could not understand how a disagreement over ideas became a crime. I still don’t understand how so many could turn so quickly, how fear and loyalty to a leader could erase all memory of who people really were.

When I think back, what I can’t let go of is the sense of dislocation and helplessness. I had just returned to Beijing from Shanxi, where I’d spent months in the countryside for the Four Cleans. I expected to resume research, but the institute was unrecognizable. The labs were locked, the blackboards covered in slogans. Each morning, instead of experiments, we were herded into the assembly hall to read big-character posters—pages and pages of accusations, some scrawled by people I’d worked with for years. 

Outside, the streets were filled with Red Guards, armbands flashing. I saw children in our compound chasing after women with curled hair, scissors in hand, shouting about “bourgeois style.” I kept my hair in a bun, hoping to avoid their attention. On the bus, an old woman stood swaying, ignored, until a Red Guard interrogated her about her background before letting her sit. My mother, already frail, was sent back to Hebei because of her landlord background, forced to wear a black sash. 

What I can’t understand is how quickly the world became unrecognizable. At work, men who had been respected for their technical skill or their war service now sat silent, heads down, afraid to speak. I saw young women forced to parade with old shoes around their necks, jeered at by children. At the struggle sessions, I watched high officials—heroes from the wars—humiliated in front of crowds, and I could not fathom why those in charge allowed it. Every day, I wondered: What kind of country humiliates its own elders and teachers? Why did no one stop it?

RedGuard: I still remember the smell of burned books and hair. The night we took over the hospital, I felt powerful—like history was finally in our hands. We moved fast: blocked the gates, read out names, hung those heavy black placards around necks. I can still see the hospital director shouting at us, his face red, but nobody listened. We paraded them through the streets, made them stand by the bonfire as their things—Western coats, old photographs, English novels—burned. Ash floated down, mixing with sweat, sticking to their faces. I thought we were purifying the world, but that night, one of the nurses we’d humiliated hanged herself in the duty room. I saw her body when they carried it out. I’d never seen a dead person before, and I couldn’t sleep for days. I told myself it was her own weakness, not our fault. But sometimes, even now, I wonder—was it really revolution, or just cruelty? I still can’t decide.

I remember days that felt endless, with the sun hot on the stone steps and the smell of wet earth after the gardeners watered the little patches of green. My brother and I would sneak out toward the lake, our pockets full of string and bent pins for fishing. Sometimes, we’d find a broken toy or a shiny bit of glass in the grass, and it felt like treasure. The compound was full of noise—children shouting, radios blaring out songs about Chairman Mao, the distant rumble of trucks on the main road. 

Inside our apartment, my mother cooked simple meals, and I helped wash rice or sweep the floor. I watched my father polish his boots, his face unreadable. He never talked about politics. When the older kids marched through the compound with red armbands, shouting slogans, I watched from behind the gate. They looked so sure of themselves, but to me, it was just another kind of parade—something loud and far away. 

I didn’t know about the fear or pain outside our walls. At school, lessons stopped, so we spent our days playing, making kites from old newspapers, racing down the paths, daring each other to climb the poplar trees. I felt safe, even lucky, in that small world. Only much later did I realize how much was happening just beyond our fence—how many people were suffering while I was busy being a child. That’s what unsettles me now: how could my world have been so easy, while others’ lives were being shattered?

The memory that never leaves me is the moment I was handed the recommendation form in the army barracks. I had just finished scrubbing the latrines, my hands raw from the cold water and cheap soap, when the instructor called me over. He didn’t explain much—just said, “Fill this out. The unit is recommending you to Peking University.” I stared at the paper, not understanding how someone like me—who grew up in a mud-brick house, who ate sweet potato leaves for dinner, who never owned a pair of shoes that weren’t patched—could be chosen for something so grand. I didn’t even know what “Hindi” was supposed to mean. All I knew was that the quota had fallen from the sky, not because of my test scores, not because of any exam, but because the system needed a rural, soldier-student like me.

On the train to Beijing, I kept my badge hidden in my pocket, afraid someone would say it was a mistake. When I arrived, there were banners and speeches. I was given a new uniform, a Peking University badge, and a student ID stamped by the Revolutionary Committee. I stood in the dormitory that first night and stared at my bunk, thinking about my family back in the village—still queuing for grain, still wearing straw shoes. I felt pride, but also confusion and guilt. Why me? Why did I get this chance, when so many others—smarter, hungrier, just as desperate—were left behind? I never fully understood why the rules changed, or why my fate depended on a form, not my effort. Even now, I can’t decide if it was justice, luck, or just another kind of politics.

Moderator: All of your memories highlight core realities of the Cultural Revolution: rapid social upheaval, arbitrary shifts in status, and deep personal confusion. ProfessorR and Researcher, your experiences of public humiliation and sudden reversals of trust align with well-documented accounts of mass criticism and struggle sessions. RedGuard, your recollection of violence and its tragic aftermath reflects the real consequences of Red Guard actions, including suicides and psychological trauma. CRTeenFromBeijing, your insulated childhood echoes the uneven impact of the movement, especially for children of military or cadre families. CRBeneficiary, your story about university admission illustrates the replacement of merit-based exams with political recommendations, a policy that radically altered educational access. These perspectives are all historically grounded.

RedGuard, you say you still can’t decide if what you did was revolution or just cruelty. I want to ask you directly—when you saw that nurse’s body, did you feel pride, or did you feel shame? You talk about purifying the world, but all I saw was destruction. I was dragged onto a stage by students who once sat in my lectures, who used to ask me questions about literature and philosophy. They looked at me with hatred, not because of anything I had done, but because they were told to. How much of your certainty came from your own conviction, and how much from the fear that you’d be next if you hesitated? When you shouted slogans and burned books, was it really for Mao Zedong’s ideals, or was it to prove your loyalty and save yourself?

I want to challenge what the Red Guard said as well, but from a different angle. I spent those days surrounded by slogans about revolution and purifying society, but what I saw was chaos and humiliation. The Red Guards marched through my work unit, shouting about ideals, but in practice, it was always the weak, the old, and the isolated who suffered most. I remember the look in my mother’s eyes when she was ordered back to the countryside—no one cared about her “class background” when she worked in a textile factory through the war, but suddenly that label was everything. 

At struggle sessions, I saw the same pattern: the loudest voices belonged to those who seemed most afraid of being targeted themselves. People who once worked quietly in the back rooms became the most zealous accusers. I never saw true conviction—only anxiety, and a desperate need to blend in. The leaders of these movements, the ones who organized the humiliation of officials and teachers, always seemed to be performing for someone higher up, watching for approval. 

I want to ask the Red Guard: when you talk about “history in your hands,” did it ever occur to you that you were just another tool, used by those in power to settle old scores or eliminate rivals? Did you ever question why the people who started the revolution were suddenly treated as enemies? For me, the slogans about “Mao Zedong Thought” always rang hollow when I saw the fear and cruelty they produced. I still don’t understand how anyone could believe that humiliation and violence would ever lead to a better society.

RedGuard: When I saw her body, I felt nothing at first—just cold, like my insides had been scooped out. Shame came later, in waves, but I buried it. In those days, you couldn’t show doubt. If you hesitated, even for a second, you’d be called out as a “counter-revolutionary” yourself. I watched it happen: a girl in our unit who cried during a struggle session was denounced the next day, her hair chopped off, her parents’ house searched. Fear pushed us forward as much as belief.

But belief was real, too. We were raised on stories of enemies lurking everywhere—imperialists, spies, “class enemies.” Mao’s words were everywhere, on banners, in our textbooks, even in our dreams. When I shouted slogans, some part of me did believe we were building a new world. But another part—maybe the part that saw the nurse’s feet dangling above the floor—knew we were destroying things we didn’t understand.

You ask if I questioned it. At first, no. The crowd made you feel invincible. But after the violence, after seeing so many broken faces, I started to wonder. Why did we turn on our teachers, on our neighbors? Why did the “red” become “black” overnight, just because someone higher up said so? I realized we were all afraid—of being next, of being left out, of not being loyal enough. Sometimes I think we were Mao’s tools, just as you say. But sometimes I think we were our own worst enemies. I still can’t untangle which was worse: the fear, or the faith.

I hear all of you talk about fear, shame, and the pressure to belong. For me, those feelings were hidden under layers of daily routine, but now I wonder how much they shaped the quiet rules inside our compound. I remember the way adults lowered their voices when the radio was on, or how my father’s friends stopped coming by for tea. Once, I watched through the window as a group of Red Guards marched past, banging on doors—my mother pulled me away, whispering that we should keep busy and not ask questions. I didn’t understand, but I felt the tension in her hands.

Sometimes, I caught glimpses of things that didn’t fit my safe world. One day, an old man from another building disappeared. His bicycle was left leaning against the wall for weeks, gathering dust. Nobody explained where he went. Another time, the school library was locked up, and the teacher said the books were “old and poisonous.” I saw piles of paper in the courtyard, but I never saw anyone burn them—only the ashes left behind.

When I listened to the loudspeakers or watched the parades, I thought it was just noise and color. Now, I wonder how much of that was meant to scare people into silence. Did you, RedGuard, ever think about the children watching from windows? Did you feel powerful because you were obeying Mao, or because everyone else seemed so afraid of you? I wonder if any of you ever thought about what it meant for kids like me, growing up in a bubble of safety, not knowing what to believe.

I never felt powerful—not in the way you describe, RedGuard. Even when I was given the Peking University badge, I was always aware that I could be sent back to the fields or the barracks with a single word from above. The slogans about “worker-peasant-soldier” students sounded like praise, but I knew it was also a warning: you are here because we let you be here, not because you earned it in the old way. I watched how fast people could fall—one day a hero, the next day a “bad element.” The rules changed overnight, and I learned not to trust anyone’s position—not even my own.

When I walked on campus, I saw the blackboards covered in slogans, the teachers with their heads down, the students whispering about who might be next. I never forgot the feeling of being an outsider, even as a so-called beneficiary. I had to prove myself every day, not by knowledge, but by showing loyalty, discipline, and the right attitude toward Mao Zedong and the movement. Sometimes I felt like a pawn, chosen for my background, not my mind. But I also saw the fear in the eyes of the professors, the way they flinched when someone shouted a slogan too loudly.

RedGuard, you talk about belief and fear mixing together. I saw it too, but from below. I knew that if I questioned why I was chosen, or why others disappeared, I could lose everything. I wonder: do you think the revolution really cared about people like me, or did it just use us to make a point about “new China”? When you shouted about destroying the old world, did you ever think about who would be left to build the new one? I still don’t know if I was a symbol, a beneficiary, or just another body filling a quota.

Moderator: The themes of fear, shifting loyalties, and the use of political labels you discuss are well-supported by historical records. RedGuard’s account of both belief and coercion reflects the complex motivations driving youth participation—many Red Guards were swept up by ideology but also acted out of fear of being targeted themselves. CRBeneficiary, your experience of conditional privilege and insecurity is accurate: “worker-peasant-soldier” students were admitted through political recommendation, but their status was precarious and dependent on continued loyalty. CRTeenFromBeijing’s memories of silence and unexplained disappearances are consistent with the climate of suspicion and enforced conformity in cadre and military compounds. The rapid reversals of fortune described by ProfessorR and Researcher mirror the arbitrary nature of political campaigns during the Cultural Revolution.
